lessonTitle: The Simple Brayton Cycle: Compressor, Combustor and Turbine

blocks.text: A land-based gas turbine generating 100 MW ingests air, squeezes it to about ten times atmospheric pressure, burns fuel in it and expands the hot gas through a turbine. Yet a large fraction of the turbine's shaft work, often 40 to 60 percent for simple gas turbines, is eaten by the compressor on the same shaft. This unit explains why, and how to estimate the numbers.

blocks.markdown: The simple **Brayton cycle** has four steady-flow processes: **1-2** isentropic compression in a compressor; **2-3** constant-pressure heat addition in a combustor; **3-4** isentropic expansion in a turbine; **4-1** constant-pressure heat rejection (to the atmosphere in an open engine). In the **cold-air-standard** analysis the working fluid is air throughout, treated as an ideal gas with constant specific heat $c_p \approx 1.005$ kJ/(kg K) and ratio $k=c_p/c_v=1.4$, and combustion is replaced by heat addition.

blocks.title: Pressure ratio
blocks.text: The pressure ratio $r_p = p_2/p_1 = p_3/p_4$ is the ratio of compressor outlet to inlet pressure (dimensionless). It is the main design variable of the ideal cycle.

blocks.caption: Isentropic ideal-gas relation applied to the compressor (1-2) and turbine (3-4)

blocks.markdown: Because every process is steady-flow with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, the energy balance on a device reduces to a change in enthalpy, and for constant $c_p$ that is $c_p\,\Delta T$. With units of kJ/kg for specific work and heat:

blocks.caption: Ideal cold-air-standard Brayton efficiency: it depends only on r_p and k

blocks.title: Brayton cycle with a pressure ratio of 8
blocks.prompt: Air enters the compressor at 300 K. The pressure ratio is 8 and the turbine inlet temperature is 1200 K. Use cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg K) and k = 1.4. Find the compressor work, turbine work, net work, thermal efficiency and back work ratio.

steps.text: Isentropic temperatures from the pressure ratio, exponent (k-1)/k = 0.2857.
Efficiency from the pressure ratio (check: net work over heat input gives the same value).

blocks.answer: w_c = 244.7, w_t = 540.2, w_net = 295.6 kJ/kg; efficiency 44.8 %; back work ratio 45.3 %.

blocks.caption: Ideal efficiency rises with pressure ratio but with diminishing returns

blocks.markdown: Where does the large compressor demand come from? Work per kilogram in a steady-flow device is proportional to the temperature change, and for the same pressure ratio the temperature change is proportional to the inlet temperature. The compressor works on cool air near 300 K, whereas the turbine expands gas at up to 1200 K or more, so the turbine produces more, but not hugely more. The compressor needs a fraction $w_c/w_t = T_2/T_3 = (T_1/T_3) r_p^{(k-1)/k}$ of the turbine work (ideal case, constant $c_p$); the pressure-ratio factor raises it above $T_1/T_3$.

blocks.caption: Back work ratio of the ideal cycle

blocks.title: Second case: higher pressure ratio
blocks.prompt: Air enters at 290 K, pressure ratio 12, turbine inlet 1400 K. Find the net work per kg.
blocks.answer: w_net = 413.9 kJ/kg, with back work ratio 42.1 %.

blocks.title: Cold-air-standard limits
blocks.text: Real gas turbines have back work ratios of about 40 to 60 %, efficiencies far below the ideal value, and variable specific heats. The ideal formula is a ceiling for the chosen pressure ratio, not a prediction.

blocks.title: Why back work matters
blocks.text: A large back work ratio makes net output a small difference of two big numbers. A small loss in compressor or turbine performance therefore causes a large drop in net work, which is why component efficiency is so important in gas turbines.

points: The ideal Brayton cycle has isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion and constant-pressure heat rejection.
Cold-air-standard efficiency is 1 - r_p^(-(k-1)/k) and depends only on the pressure ratio.
Compressor and turbine work follow from cp times the temperature change across each device.
The back work ratio T1 r_p^((k-1)/k)/T3 is large because compression is done on cold air while expansion is done on hot gas.

questions.stem: In the ideal cold-air-standard Brayton cycle, which change increases the thermal efficiency?

options.text: Raising the pressure ratio
Raising only the turbine inlet temperature
Lowering the compressor inlet temperature only
Using a larger mass flow rate

distractorRationale.b: T3 does not appear in the ideal efficiency formula.
distractorRationale.c: T1 cancels in the efficiency expression.
distractorRationale.d: Mass flow scales power, not efficiency.

questions.explanation: The ideal efficiency is 1 - r_p^(-(k-1)/k), so only the pressure ratio and k matter. A larger pressure ratio shrinks the second term and raises efficiency.

questions.stem: A student says the ideal Brayton efficiency should rise when the turbine inlet temperature is raised from 1100 K to 1400 K at a fixed pressure ratio. What is the best response?

options.text: Correct: more heat is added, so efficiency must rise
Incorrect: the ideal efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio, although net work per kg rises
Incorrect: efficiency falls because the compressor work rises
Correct: efficiency equals the ratio T3/T1

questions.correctOptionText: Incorrect: the ideal efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio, although net work per kg rises

distractorRationale.a: Net work rises, but efficiency in the ideal cycle is unchanged.
distractorRationale.c: Compressor work is set by T1 and r_p, not T3.
distractorRationale.d: That is not the Brayton efficiency formula.

questions.explanation: For the ideal cycle the efficiency equals 1 - 1/r_p^((k-1)/k), with no T3 dependence. Raising T3 increases both heat input and net work in proportion so that the ratio stays the same, although the work output per kilogram of air increases.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the specific work output of the turbine in the cold-air-standard analysis?

options.text: cp (T4 - T3)
cp (T3 - T4)
cp (T2 - T1)
cp (T3 - T2)

distractorRationale.a: Sign reversed: this is negative for an expansion.
distractorRationale.c: That is the compressor work input.
distractorRationale.d: That is the heat added in the combustor.

questions.explanation: The steady-flow energy balance for an adiabatic turbine gives w = h3 - h4, which for constant cp is cp (T3 - T4). The other expressions describe the compressor work or the heat input.

questions.stem: Why is the back work ratio of a gas turbine cycle much larger than that of a steam power cycle?

options.text: The compressor handles a gas, so it needs a large volume change and so a large work input per kg
Gas turbines are always less efficient components than steam turbines
The combustor absorbs part of the turbine work
Gas turbines run at lower pressure ratios

questions.correctOptionText: The compressor handles a gas, so it needs a large volume change and so a large work input per kg

distractorRationale.b: Efficiency of components is not the fundamental reason.
distractorRationale.c: The combustor has no shaft work.
distractorRationale.d: The pressure ratio is not lower; the fluid being compressed is a gas, not a liquid.

questions.explanation: Compressing a gas requires significant work because its specific volume is large, whereas pumping a liquid needs very little. In the Brayton cycle the compressor therefore absorbs a large share of the turbine output.

questions.stem: An ideal Brayton cycle runs at a fixed pressure ratio and compressor inlet temperature. The maximum cycle temperature T3 is reduced (for example by a material limit). What happens to the back work ratio?

options.text: It falls because less fuel is burned
It stays the same because the pressure ratio is unchanged
It rises because the turbine produces less work while the compressor work is unchanged
It falls because the compressor work falls with T3

questions.correctOptionText: It rises because the turbine produces less work while the compressor work is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Back work ratio is not tied to fuel directly.
distractorRationale.b: It depends on T1/T3 as well as the pressure ratio.
distractorRationale.d: Compressor work is independent of T3.

questions.explanation: The back work ratio is (T1/T3) r_p^((k-1)/k), so lowering T3 increases it. The compressor work is fixed by T1 and r_p, while turbine work falls as T3 falls.

questions.stem: An ideal cold-air-standard Brayton cycle (k = 1.4) has a pressure ratio of 15. Find the thermal efficiency as a decimal fraction (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The efficiency is 1 - 15^(-0.2857) = 1 - 0.4613 = 0.5387. This is the ideal ceiling for that pressure ratio.

questions.stem: Air enters the compressor of an ideal Brayton cycle at 290 K. The pressure ratio is 10 and the turbine inlet temperature is 1300 K. Use cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg K) and k = 1.4. Find the net specific work in kJ/kg.
A gas turbine ideal cycle has compressor inlet 288 K, pressure ratio 12, turbine inlet temperature 1100 K, k = 1.4 and constant cp. Find the back work ratio w_c / w_t as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The ideal back work ratio is (T1/T3) r_p^0.2857 = (288/1100) x 2.0339 = 0.5325, i.e. 53.3 %. More than half of the turbine output goes to driving the compressor.

questions.stem: Explain, in terms of temperature and specific volume, why a large fraction of the turbine work in a simple gas turbine is absorbed by the compressor. State how the fraction varies with maximum cycle temperature.
markingGuide: Steady-flow work per unit mass is proportional to the temperature change, which for the same pressure ratio scales with inlet temperature
Compressor handles cool dense air at T1; turbine handles hot gas at T3 so its work is larger only by the factor T3/T2 (w_t/w_c = T3/T2, the reciprocal of the back work ratio)
Compression work is large because a gas has large specific volume (unlike pumping a liquid)
Back work ratio = w_c/w_t = T2/T3 = (T1/T3) r^((k-1)/k) so it falls as T3 rises
Net work is a small difference of two large quantities so component losses matter
questions.explanation: The compressor and the turbine experience the same pressure ratio, but the turbine gas is hotter, so it produces more work in proportion to T3/T2 (w_t/w_c = T3/T2, with T2 = T1 r_p^((k-1)/k)). The back work ratio therefore shrinks as the turbine inlet temperature rises.

questions.stem: Describe the four processes of the ideal Brayton cycle, state the cold-air-standard assumptions, and explain why raising the pressure ratio raises the ideal efficiency.
markingGuide: Assumes air as an ideal gas with constant cp and k, combustion replaced by heat addition
Efficiency = 1 - r_p^(-(k-1)/k); larger r_p reduces the exponent term so efficiency rises (higher mean heat addition temperature)
questions.explanation: The ideal cycle is fully described by two isentropes and two isobars. Because the efficiency expression decreases its loss term as r_p increases, a higher pressure ratio always raises ideal efficiency, though with diminishing returns.
